text:
The Dreame cloud protocol is NOT vendored into this repo. init.py downloads protocol.py, types.py and exceptions.py from Tasshack/dreame-vacuum at a SHA pinned in init.py UPSTREAM_SHA.

Two alternatives were considered and rejected by the repo owner:
  - Vendoring the files (upstream is MIT, so it was legally fine). Rejected: we would own keeping them current, and the repo would carry someone else's 285KB of code.
  - Tracking the dev branch tip, which is what the original proof-of-concept script did. Rejected: upstream could break the plugin at any time with no warning.

The pin has a cost that is easy to miss: protocol.py contains an obfuscated blob holding the Dreame API host, port, app User-Agent, Basic auth header and password salt. Pinning the code therefore also freezes those endpoint constants. If login starts failing across the board for no apparent reason, the fix is to bump UPSTREAM_SHA, not to debug our code.

Cleaning mode detection deliberately does NOT read upstream's per-model capability table.

Upstream decides mop-pad-lifting from an obfuscated DEVICE_INFO table (const.py) loaded by DreameVacuumDeviceCapability.load, which raises 'Unsupported Device!' for any model not in it. Depending on that would make the plugin fail on new models for no good reason, and would mean shipping a model list we have to maintain.

Instead we use upstream's own fallback derivation: mop_pad_lifting = self_wash_base AND auto_empty_base, probed as the presence of properties 4/25 and 15/3. This is one of four disjuncts upstream ORs together, so a lifting model with no self-wash base would be misdetected and would get sweep and sweep_and_mop exchanged. Accepted as a known limitation, documented in the README.

Confirmed correct on the owner's dreame.vacuum.r2416a (X40 Ultra) against the Dreame app: raw packed value 0x1400 with lifting detected reads as 'sweep and mop', and the app agreed. Writing sweep produced 0x1402 (wire 2, the swap) with the self-clean field in bits 8-15 still 20, so bit preservation works on real hardware. That self-clean setting is exactly what the original proof-of-concept would have destroyed by writing a bare 0/1/2.

Deliberately out of scope for this plugin, so nobody re-derives the reasoning:

Room and zone cleaning, and map images. Neither is reachable with a plain get_properties call: room identity only exists inside MAP_DATA (6/1), which needs upstream's map.py decoder and pulls in mini-racer, numpy and pillow. Out of proportion for a plugin whose tools must finish in 30 seconds.

More than one vacuum per account. The tools error out and list the names rather than guessing. The owner has one robot; add it when that changes.

Suction level and water volume control, schedules, consumables, and MQTT live updates. No demand yet.

The Xiaomi (non-Dreame) cloud path. Devices registered to a Dreame account have no local miIO token, so only the Dreame cloud path matters here.

The tool granularity in this plugin is driven entirely by the runner's hard 30-second kill, not by taste.

Upstream login() has a hardcoded 10-second timeout we cannot pass a value to, and it recurses once on a refresh-token error body, so a single login call is worst-case 20 seconds. That leaves room for only two or three HTTP round trips per tool. Consequences visible across the codebase:

  - set_cleaning_mode is a separate tool from start_cleaning. Setting a mode needs read-modify-write plus the start action, which is four round trips and does not fit. Do not merge them.
  - Every cloud call passes retry_count=0. Upstream defaults to retry_count=2 with a 6-second timeout, which is 18 seconds for one logical call.
  - upstream get_devices() is reimplemented locally because it hardcodes those retry defaults with no way to override them.

If someone later raises TOOL_DEADLINE_SECONDS or adds a round trip to a tool, they need to redo this arithmetic. requests applies its timeout to connect and read separately, so a single request can take about twice its nominal timeout.
